Doctor-Led Acne Care Jaipur • Sikar • Ajmer

Acne Treatment in Jaipur | Doctor-Led Care for Pimples

Acne starts when hair follicles become blocked with oil and dead skin, forming blackheads and whiteheads; bacteria and inflammation can then turn them into red pimples and cysts. It is common and treatable. At Kezza, our skin doctors examine your skin and build a plan of medicines, medical peels and a simple routine at our Jaipur, Sikar and Ajmer clinics.

Understanding Acne

What Causes Acne?

Acne treatment clears pimples and lowers the chance of marks and scars by unblocking pores, calming inflammation and reducing oil. Mild acne usually responds to prescription creams and gels; moderate or severe acne may need tablets, medical peels or isotretinoin. It takes at least six to eight weeks to see fewer breakouts.

Every hair follicle on the face, chest and back is connected to an oil gland. Acne begins when extra oil (sebum) and dead skin cells block the opening of a follicle. A blocked pore that stays closed is a whitehead; one that opens to the air darkens and becomes a blackhead.

Inside a blocked pore, bacteria that normally live on the skin can multiply, and the body reacts with inflammation. That creates red papules, pus-filled pustules and, when the inflammation runs deep, painful nodules and cysts. These deep, inflamed spots are the ones most likely to leave marks and scars.

Hormones play a large part, which is why acne often starts in the teenage years and can flare around periods or with conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Some medicines, heavy or oily cosmetics and hair products, and picking or squeezing spots can also make acne worse.

In Short:

  • Blocked pores: oil and dead skin clog the follicle.
  • Inflammation: turns blocked pores into red spots and cysts.
  • Early treatment: lowers the chance of marks and scars.
Treatment Options

How Acne Is Treated at Kezza

Creams & Gels

Prescription retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid or antibiotic gels, chosen for your type of acne and your skin.

Tablets

For moderate to severe acne, a limited course of antibiotic tablets or, for some women, hormonal treatment, used with creams.

Isotretinoin

For severe or scarring acne that has not responded to other treatment, isotretinoin prescribed and monitored by a doctor.

Medical Peels

Salicylic acid and other peels to unclog pores and calm breakouts, repeated every few weeks alongside medicines.

Extraction & Cyst Care

Careful removal of stubborn blackheads and whiteheads, and an injection to settle a painful cyst when needed.

Daily Routine

A simple routine of gentle cleanser, non-comedogenic moisturiser and sunscreen that works with your treatment.

When to See a Doctor

When Should You See a Doctor for Acne?

Mild acne often improves with over-the-counter products, but some acne needs prescription treatment to prevent marks and scars.

Book a consultation if

  • Your acne has not improved after two to three months of over-the-counter products
  • You have painful nodules or cysts, or spots that leave dark marks or dents
  • Acne is affecting your confidence, work or daily life
  • You have acne with irregular periods, extra facial hair or sudden weight change, which can point to a hormonal cause

Tell your doctor if

  • You are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding; several acne medicines are not safe then
  • You take other medicines, including steroids, which can affect acne
  • You have used isotretinoin, antibiotics or hormonal treatment for acne before
  • You have sensitive skin, eczema or rosacea, which changes the choice of products

Once breakouts are under control, marks and scars can be treated. See our acne scar treatment page for the options.

Your Visit

What Happens at Your Acne Consultation

Your first visit sets a plan you can follow at home, with reviews to adjust it.

01

Skin Examination

Your doctor looks at the type and pattern of your spots, checks for marks and scars, and asks about your skin care, periods, medicines and past treatments.

02

Finding Triggers

Hormonal patterns, cosmetics, sweat, friction from helmets or masks, and medicines that may be making acne worse are identified.

03

Your Treatment Plan

You get a treatment plan with prescription creams, tablets if needed, and clear instructions on using them to limit dryness and irritation.

04

In-Clinic Treatment

Medical peels or extraction may be added to speed up clearing, spaced a few weeks apart.

05

Review & Maintenance

Progress is reviewed after 6 to 8 weeks, and a maintenance plan helps keep new breakouts away.

Timeline

Acne Treatment Timeline

Acne treatment works slowly, so keep going long enough to judge it fairly.

W1

First Weeks

Some dryness or peeling from creams is common, and your doctor will show you how to manage it.

W4

Around Week 4

New spots can still appear; this does not mean the treatment is failing.

W8

Weeks 6 to 8

Most people start to see fewer breakouts.

M3

Months 2 to 3

Many treatments show a clear effect by now, and the plan is adjusted if needed.

M6

Maintenance

A maintenance treatment, often a retinoid, helps keep skin clear once acne is controlled.

Medical Note: Results vary from person to person. This page is general information from Kezza Hair & Skin Clinic and is not a substitute for a consultation with a doctor.

Types of acne

  • Comedonal acne: mainly blackheads and whiteheads, often on the forehead, nose and chin. Retinoids and salicylic acid are the usual first steps.
  • Inflammatory acne: red papules and pus-filled spots. Creams that reduce bacteria and inflammation are combined, and tablets are added if it is widespread.
  • Nodular and cystic acne: deep, painful lumps that are the most likely to scar. This type needs prompt treatment with a doctor, and the American Academy of Dermatology notes that isotretinoin is used for nodular acne that has not responded to other treatment.
  • Hormonal acne: often along the jawline and chin in adult women, sometimes with irregular periods. Hormonal treatments can help alongside skin treatment.

Using acne creams without irritation

Retinoids and benzoyl peroxide work well, but they can make the skin dry, red or flaky in the first few weeks, which is the most common reason people stop. A few simple habits help. Use a pea-sized amount for the whole face rather than dabbing it only on spots, because acne treatment is about preventing new spots as well as clearing existing ones. Start every other night if your skin is sensitive, apply a plain moisturiser, and wear sunscreen during the day because some treatments make the skin more sensitive to the sun. If irritation does not settle, tell your doctor rather than stopping; the product or the way you use it can be changed.

Acne and dark marks in Indian skin

In brown skin, a pimple often leaves a flat dark mark behind after it heals. These marks, called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, are not scars, and they usually fade over several months once breakouts stop. Controlling acne early is the best way to prevent them. Sun protection helps marks fade faster, and your doctor may suggest ingredients such as azelaic acid or a course of medical peels. Squeezing or picking spots makes marks darker and longer-lasting, and can turn a mark into a scar.

Everyday habits that help

  • Wash your face twice a day and after sweating with a gentle, non-soap cleanser; scrubbing harder does not clear acne faster.
  • Keep hair oils and heavy styling products away from the forehead and face.
  • Choose non-comedogenic moisturiser, sunscreen and makeup.
  • Do not pick, squeeze or pop spots, especially deep ones.
  • Take medicines exactly as prescribed and finish the course your doctor advises.

Why patients choose Kezza for acne care

  • Doctor-led: our doctors examine your skin, find your acne type and triggers, and prescribe and review your medicines.
  • Marks and scars in the same plan: once breakouts settle, dark marks and scars can be treated without changing clinics.
  • Gentle on Indian skin: treatments start gently and build up, to avoid irritation that can leave new dark marks.
  • Three clinics: Jaipur, Sikar and Ajmer, open 9 AM to 8 PM every day, which makes regular reviews easier.
  • Clear costs: the plan and the expected costs are explained at your consultation.

What affects the cost of acne treatment?

The cost depends on the medicines you need, whether in-clinic treatments such as peels are added, and how many review visits your plan includes. Mild acne may only need a consultation, prescription creams and a follow-up, while severe acne usually needs longer treatment and closer monitoring. Your doctor explains the plan before you start.

FAQs

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does acne treatment take to work?
Longer than most people expect. The American Academy of Dermatology says it takes at least 6 to 8 weeks to start seeing fewer breakouts, and the NHS notes that many treatments take 2 to 3 months to work. Stopping too early is one of the most common reasons acne treatment seems not to work.
Will acne go away on its own?
Mild acne often settles with time and good skin care, but moderate to severe acne can last for years and leave marks and scars if it is not treated. Starting effective treatment early is the best way to protect your skin.
Is isotretinoin safe?
Isotretinoin is very effective for severe acne, but it has important side effects and must be supervised by a doctor. It must not be taken during pregnancy, so women need reliable contraception during treatment and for a time afterwards. Your doctor will explain the checks and follow-up needed before you start.
Do chemical peels help with acne?
Medical peels such as salicylic acid can unclog pores and reduce breakouts when they are used alongside medicines, and they can help fade marks. They are usually repeated every few weeks. On their own, they do not control the underlying causes of acne.
Can I wear makeup if I have acne?
Yes. Choose products labelled non-comedogenic or oil-free, remove makeup gently every night, and avoid heavy, oily products on the areas where you break out. Your doctor can suggest products that suit your treatment.
Why do I still get acne as an adult?
Adult acne is common, especially in women, and is often linked to hormones, stress or products used on the skin and hair. It usually appears on the lower face and jawline. It responds to treatment, which may include creams, peels and, for some women, hormonal medicines.
Will my acne marks fade after treatment?
Flat dark or red marks usually fade over the months after breakouts stop, and faster with daily sunscreen and treatment; mild dark marks often fade within six to twelve months. Marks that leave the skin pitted or raised are scars. See our pigmentation treatment page for dark marks and our acne scar treatment page for scars.
When should I see a doctor about acne?
See a doctor if products from the chemist have not helped after a few weeks of regular use, if you have painful lumps or cysts, if your acne is leaving dark marks or scars, or if it is affecting your confidence. Treating acne early is the most reliable way to prevent scars.
